raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide transient coronary support and antiproliferative drug delivery while avoiding the permanent “metallic cage” of drug-eluting stents (DES). The theoretical advantages were compelling: late restoration of vasomotion, adaptive remodelling, easier non-invasive imaging, preserved surgical options, and potentially fewer very-late adverse events. Early first-in-human studies of the poly-L-lactic-acid everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold showed procedural feasibility, acceptable early safety, and imaging signals of late lumen enlargement and vasomotor recovery [1], [2]. Iterative changes improved radial strength and drug delivery, and early cohort studies supported further randomized evaluation [3], [4]. Pathological and imaging studies, however, also highlighted delayed healing, bulky struts, and the importance of complete scaffold apposition during a prolonged resorption process [5].

The first generation of clinically tested BVS was dominated by the Absorb everolimus-eluting scaffold, with approximately 150-µm struts and limited overexpansion capacity. In ABSORB II, BVS did not demonstrate superior vasomotion or late lumen outcomes compared with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents, and longer follow-up revealed excess target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis [6], [7]. ABSORB III initially met non-inferiority for target-lesion failure at 1 year, but subsequent analyses identified higher event rates, particularly in small vessels and when implantation technique was suboptimal [8]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China broadly confirmed short-term efficacy in selected lesions but did not dispel safety concerns [9], [10]. ABSORB IV, designed with more rigorous implantation technique and exclusion of very small vessels, reduced but did not eliminate the clinical penalty versus metallic DES [11]. In the pragmatic AIDA trial, routine BVS use was associated with significantly more device thrombosis, leading to early safety warnings and withdrawal of Absorb from commercial use [12].

The signal was consistent across broader randomized evidence. EVERBIO II, TROFI II, and STEMI registries suggested that BVS could be implanted successfully in selected patients, including some with acute myocardial infarction, but they did not establish superiority over contemporary DES [13], [14], [15]. Meta-analyses and patient-level pooled analyses subsequently showed higher definite or probable device thrombosis and target-lesion failure with Absorb, especially during the first 3 years when scaffold mass persisted [16], [17], [18]. These findings reframed the concept: bioresorption alone was not sufficient; scaffold geometry, mechanical properties, lesion selection, and implantation quality were decisive determinants of outcomes.

Mechanistically, adverse events were multifactorial. Thick struts increased flow disturbance and thrombogenicity, particularly in small vessels or bifurcations. Polymer recoil, underexpansion, malapposition, edge dissection, and discontinuity during late dismantling contributed to scaffold thrombosis [19], [20]. Optical coherence tomography studies clarified that aggressive lesion preparation, accurate sizing, high-pressure post-dilatation, and avoidance of small reference vessels were essential [21], [22]. This “PSP” approach—prepare the lesion, size appropriately, and post-dilate—became central to BVS practice. Prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy was also commonly recommended during the active resorption phase, although the optimal duration was never definitively established.

BVS experience also stimulated development of alternative platforms. The DESolve novolimus-eluting scaffold sought improved expansion tolerance and self-correction of malapposition [23]. Magnesium-based scaffolds offered faster resorption and potentially lower chronic inflammatory burden. The first-generation drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffold in BIOSOLVE-I demonstrated feasibility, while the second-generation sirolimus-eluting magnesium scaffold showed improved angiographic performance in BIOSOLVE-II and encouraging larger-registry outcomes in BIOSOLVE-IV [24], [25], [26]. Other polymeric platforms, including Fantom, explored thinner struts, radiopacity, and different resorption kinetics, but none has yet displaced modern ultrathin metallic DES in routine PCI [27].

Current clinical lessons are clear. First, the benchmark is demanding: contemporary DES are safe, deliver low restenosis rates, and have very low late thrombosis rates. Second, BVS should not be judged as a class solely by the failure of one scaffold, but future devices must demonstrate not merely bioresorption, but DES-level early safety before any hypothesized late benefit can emerge. Third, trials must use optimized implantation, intravascular imaging, adequate vessel size thresholds, and long-term follow-up beyond complete resorption [28], [29]. Finally, the most plausible future niches may be younger patients with large, simple lesions; situations where future surgical grafting or repeat PCI is likely; or hybrid strategies using transient scaffolding in selected segments rather than routine whole-lesion replacement [30].

In summary, BVS transformed thinking about PCI by challenging the assumption that permanent implants are necessary after coronary revascularization. The first commercial polymeric scaffold failed because theoretical late advantages were outweighed by early and midterm safety hazards. Yet the biological rationale remains attractive. The next generation must combine thin struts, sufficient radial strength, predictable degradation, excellent deliverability, radiographic visibility, and outcomes proven against best-in-class DES in adequately powered trials.
